claims.text: The component material is susceptible to hot cracking when fusion-welded because of its microstructural characteristics.
The damaged component retains enough integrity to be repaired.
Friction stir processing can restore the damaged region without initiating the hot cracking typical of fusion welding.
An FSP-repaired component will perform comparably to or better than a fusion-weld-repaired component under aggressive operating conditions.
Controlled tool speed, force, and temperature can keep the FSP repair below the material's melting temperature.
FSP produces a localized, refined, dynamically recrystallized microstructure in the stirred zone.
Avoiding a molten phase prevents the microsegregation associated with hot cracking.
Mechanical stirring and plastic deformation below fusion-welding temperatures create a solid-state bond.
Preventing formation of a liquid phase avoids hot cracking.
FSP-induced grain refinement enhances mechanical properties.
FSP repairs will have fewer or no hot cracks relative to conventional fusion-welded repairs.
FSP repairs will provide equal or improved mechanical performance under high thermal and mechanical loads relative to conventional fusion-welded repairs.
FSP repair will improve component reliability and extend service life.
Traditional fusion repair of the damaged part causes hot cracking and compromised mechanical performance under aggressive operating conditions.
FSP repair is expected to be effective only within a process window that keeps the material below its melting temperature.
Thermal cycling and high-load testing can represent relevant intended-service conditions for validation.
